Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) for Addiction

Cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT, is one of the most widely used talk therapies in addiction treatment. The idea behind it is simple. The way you think shapes how you feel and what you do, so if you change the thinking and the triggers around it, you change the behaviour. For someone trying to stop drinking, using drugs, or gambling, that shift is often the difference between a plan that holds and one that falls apart.

blocks.text: CBT is practical and structured. It spends less time on the distant past and more on what is keeping the behaviour going right now, and what to do about it.

blocks.text: How CBT works for addiction

Addiction runs on patterns. A feeling or a situation acts as a trigger, an automatic thought follows, such as “I can’t cope without it” or “one won’t hurt”, and the urge to use takes over. CBT breaks that chain down so you can see it clearly, then works on each link. You learn to catch the thought, question it, and choose a different response before the urge wins.

blocks.text: What happens in a CBT session
blocks.html: What happens in a CBT session

blocks.text: Sessions are collaborative. You and the therapist look at recent situations where you used or wanted to, map out what set them off, and practise specific skills for next time. There is usually some homework between sessions, like tracking triggers or trying a coping strategy in real life. Most people work through a set number of sessions rather than open-ended therapy.

blocks.text: CBT and other therapies

CBT is often combined with other approaches. Dialectical behaviour therapy, or DBT, grew out of CBT and adds a stronger focus on managing intense emotions, which helps people whose use is tied to emotional overwhelm. If you want to see how the two compare, our guide on dialectical vs cognitive behavioural therapy breaks it down.

blocks.text: What CBT helps with

CBT has strong evidence behind it for alcohol and drug addiction, and it is also a first-line treatment for behavioural addictions like gambling. It works well alongside medication, support groups, and, when needed, residential or outpatient treatment.

blocks.text: Getting CBT in Ontario

blocks.text: Frequently asked questions
How long does CBT take? Many people see results in a structured course of sessions rather than years of therapy, though it varies by person and goal.
blocks.html: How long does CBT take? Many people see results in a structured course of sessions rather than years of therapy, though it varies by person and goal.

blocks.text: Does CBT work for addiction? Yes. It is one of the best-studied therapies for substance use and behavioural addictions, and it is especially useful for preventing relapse.
blocks.html: Does CBT work for addiction? Yes. It is one of the best-studied therapies for substance use and behavioural addictions, and it is especially useful for preventing relapse.

blocks.text: Is CBT the same as DBT? No. DBT is a form of CBT that puts more emphasis on managing emotions and distress. Both can help with addiction.
